text:
NewEgg-Gigabyte 9070XT Inventory Debacle:
I got messed over by NewEgg and/or Gigabyte this morning. After staying up super late and waking up super early, spamming online stores for inventory to appear and subsequently attempting to purchase a couple different $600 9070XT models only to receive an out-of-stock notification during processing, I was finally able to purchase the “GIGABYTE Gaming Radeon RX 9070 XT 16GB GDDR6 PCI Express 5.0 x16 Graphcis Card GV-R9070XTGAMING OC-16GD.” 
Yesterday I set up a Trade-in for my current GPU in preparation for the upgrade. My transaction was completed this morning (3/6/2025) prior to 8:30AM Central Time. 
I received three emails from NewEgg this morning:
1. 8:29AM “We received your Trade-in Form”
2. 8:59AM “Order confirmed: Newegg order #577… (1 item)
3. 9:05AM “Order cancelled due to insufficient stock”
Apparently, it took NewEgg 30 full minutes to process my order. By that time—unbeknownst to me—my GPU was sold to another customer (possibly someone who did not have a trade-in offer). Meanwhile, I went about my day, thinking that I had secured my GPU and allowing 100% of all 9070XT models to be depleted. So now I have no GPU coming, and I have the pleasure of hoping NewEgg will honor the purchase agreement so that I won’t have to pay an additional $100 (who knows?) whenever inventory is replenished.
Make this right, NewEgg!

text:
While raw performance benchmarks are interesting to see well, the raw performance, it'd also be nice to see some real world playability optimized results to account for performance breakpoints.

For example, my 2080 can run some games just fine (i.e. Baldur's Gate 3) at 1080p native, but absolutely not at 4k with DLSS in performance mode, despite internally rendering at 1080p thanks  to the small 8GB VRAM buffer. That's a bit of a shame on a 4k display. Meanwhile my previous card, the RX570 8GB never really could take advantage of it's "large at the time" identical 8GB VRAM buffer, because it was so much weaker in compute than the 2080 and was basically stuck at 1080p, with a noticeably penalty for playing in ultrawide. 

So seeing benchmarks of new cards that may be a bit VRAM limited not being tested using any of the upscaling modes, is a bit "meh" to me, since I firsthand know that upscaling can look great (esp. with DLSS 4 or FSR 4) when it works, but have some performance and VRAM cost that can totally go over certain VRAM size breakpoints which would make some games perform a lot worse. And that is despite native 1440p or 1080p results looking great and 4k results just not being relevant to that performance tier. 

I really doubt many people will be choosing to play in native modes in single player titles beyond 2025 in any games that offer it, and even frame generation (thanks LosslessScaling and Optiscaler) is basically just an assumed thing (that has a cost to the assumed required base frame rate and VRAM). I personally run 2x or 3x frame generation in any title that gives me a high enough base framerate for the kind of latency hit I'm willing to accept in return for the extra smoothness.

text:
Well I dont know. It seems to me that AMD is trying (maybe even hard), but the watts needed to get the same performance as nvidia are laughable. Why is there like 50-100 watt difference against 5070? That cant be tied to the 4gb more vram right? While nvidia trolls all games by limiting vram and cutting down performance on purpose. Imagine what the 5070 could do with 16 gigs of ram 256 bus and same 300-310 watt power draw like the 9070 XT it would be basically 5080 on steroids. In the past I did not care about it because we had cheap electricity in my country and you may find that laughable, but I did some numbers and it turned out that if I buy more expensive nvidia gpu it will cost the same/less like cheaper amd in the life-cycle cost with higher electricity bill.
For this scenario I used this formula 200W/300W 5 hour a day for a year. Difference was USD 40 each year. For average lifespan of gpu before upgrading 3-5 years the difference in cost is USD 120-200. And I gotta tell you I'm afraid that 5 hours each day on average is very underestimated estimate. If you bump that up to 10 hours a day on average we are talking about USD 80 difference each year making it USD 240-400 difference in 3-5 year lifespan.
So in my case I have to buy AMD card with the same performance as nvidia for 200-300 USD less to make it reasonable choice and thats why nvidia wins for me although I really hate them how they treat gamers which help them grown since day one...

text:
Not really... And I say that as an XTX owner. I'm perfectly happy with it and knew exactly what I was buying, coming from a 6700XT and an RX580 before that. AMD is on the right track here: Invest in the software stack. Invest in getting studios to optimize for AMD. Get positive reviews for offering good value, just as the first Ryzen generations did. They need to crowbar their way into the market. And the best angle of attack is that lots of "loyal" Nvidia users are absolutely repulsed by how Nvidia is re-contexturalizing the GPU market: The halo products aren't halo products any more. They are the new normal, and if you can't afford that you deserve to be shat on like the peasant you are. If can only pay a compromised price you will only get a compromised experience you annoying little tightwad...

...All while not understanding that we are in a massive salary recession. Back in the 90s the income-to-disposable-cash ratio was a LOT different than it is now. A top shelf GPU was a nice little luxury a gamer, who worked a cash register, could splurge on themselves. Now a top shelf GPU is more than food for two-three month for a lot of people. I'm not thrilled at the price of the 9070XT, to be honest, but at least it's not outright revolting. Adjusted for inflation it's a 6.5% price creep over the 6700XT, but for double the performance (quire precisely actually) and 16GB of VRAM. Post roughly 2010 and to present date, that is outright good. But only seen in isolation. RX 6000 was too expensive, and RX 7000 didn't reel it back in. So we are seeing a good result on a bad foundation. BUT... reading the comments on a couple of reviews I see optimism. I see exactly "Good that AMD at least did SOMETHING in this awful market". Not having a hugely expensive model to compare to strangely helps in this context.

text:
The real regrettable thing is that prosumers and freelancers are forced to support Nvidia because the software they are using is optimized for CUDA or simply doesn't support Vulkan, even though there is equally capable hardware. Maybe, with AV1 coming to prominence, streamers might actually choose something from AMD for cost savings. Though, it's annoying when software doesn't work on GPUs that have largely the same feature stack simply due to lack of market share. 

Here, AMD is the better choice (at MSRP) if you are looking at the 70 level cards from Nvidia, IMO, especially if you were looking at the 5070ti. Yes, there is a significant jump in performance, and a staggering jump in ray tracing. Yet, when it's a better option to get a used 4080 super on the used market, it's harder to justify less performance and more importantly less vram for more money. Undoubtedly, AMD will have similar issues with pricing, but if they can stay within $50 to $100 of their MSRP, its still their win, though by a much smaller margin. Given the current used prices of the 7900xt and XTX, the 9070xt seems to also be the better buy, though you lose out on some v ram. Obviously, RT is going to be difficult to run on AMD, but I would be curious to know the stats of who plays games with RT enabled. I would imagine it's the majority of gamers (again, market share) but due to the performance hit and the typically greater desire for high framerate (because they paid good money for a high refresh rate monitor), it would be a very interesting talking point. Regardless, RT performance seems to be the biggest downside. Power draw is higher, typical of AMD cards, but at least it's only drawing about 300w. Given that the 16 pin connector is maxing out around 300w safely, we should continue observing the 16 pin connector closely.

TLDR
Nvidia bad and lie to consumer. AMD  less money. 5070 no is 4090. 9070xt better for wallet.

text:
Never upgrade your GPU unless you get twice the performance. Anything less is simply not worth it unless you are outright struggling to meet minimum spec in the games you want to play. But if you upgrade with the intention of splitting your new power somewhat evenly between better FPS and better visuals, you need twice the power to see gains better than "If I look closely, I guess". Techpowerup has clocked the 9070XT at exactly twice the power of a 6700XT in raster, while also making RT Medium/High viable at 1440p. That's a worthy upgrade. 

If we adjust for inflation this is only a 6.5% price creep model-for-model. But since it goes from 12GB to 16GB GDDR6 (which has also gone up in price) I think it's fair to call it price parity. Double the performance for the same price two generations later is outright good these days.

text: I've found that while game benchmarks like for XIV are often enough to get an idea of what your experience is going to be in the future, improvements likely in the drivers, or even in the software over time, either increase the in-game performance or possibly reduce the benchmark performance, since these benchmark tools are released and then often abandoned. Square cares a little more about their benchmark tool than some others, but I'm not sure even they would update it so much that it would negate this. I'd really advise just making a free account and finding somewhere consistent to plop yourself down at. The aetheryte in Limsa is always the one people go to to see how deeply the amount of players on screen can weigh down the FPS, and then you can always go to an Inn in-game which will have no other players and spin the camera or something. Of course there's all sorts of complications with benching MMO's, and maybe it's worth waiting until a week or two from now to see what the players report.

I'm really confused on why you went with a 6950 for all of the performance tests, and then power tests you went with 6600s.  That doesn't even make sense.  Use the same cards, especially for many of us who have 6700s 6800s and 6900s.  Also, only did them with RT on?  WTF?

Power usage is super important, and AMD dropped the ball entirely on this card.  310 for less power ( even if relatively marginal in some tests ) when it's competition does 205?!

Even considering the initial cost differences between the cards, a general 60 watt difference, with someone who plays 4 hours a day, 5 days a week, 52 weeks a year with high power bills of 0.50c a kwh is going to see at least $30 extra per year in costs, and some of those tests were showing the nvidia card as low as 100 watts less, so it's closer to $50 a year.  So even if getting a 5070ti costs you an extra $200  .. you'll have spent that anyway on the AMD card by the time you think about replacing either one ( and if you have an nvidia card, and RT is important, you're not likely to replace it with an AMD card in the next 4 years. )

Losing out on RT performance for just the cost is insane .. especially when the card can do 2x the frames for the same net pricepoint.  And that's the real joke here, because we're praising the 5070 here ...as being the more cost efficient card, with all the lies around it from Nvidia.  They don't deserve your money from all that .. but godamn why tf would I get an AMD card just to kid myself into thinking it's cheaper / almost the same power.  It's just not, especially with actual power usage.  Something I always praised AMD about, and the reason I went with their cards .. they were always more power efficient.  

This is a travesty.. and the bad reporting on it is part of it.   Things could flip all the way around if we knew what the NON RT efficiencies were for AMD cards that were on the list for 90% of the video.  The heck Steve.

And we haven't even gotten into the noise part of the equations.   200 watts, 50c temps, and inaudible fans can be a huge deal breaker compared to 310 watts / 85c temps in the summer, and a jet engine screaming at you.

text:
Thanks! I purposefully watched Digital Foundry's FSR3/FSR4/DLSS3/DLSS4 coverage before looking at this.

Although FSR4 is hugely better than FSR3 (perhaps slightly better than DLSS3 too!), I'd argue the gap between DLSS4 and FSR4 is greater than it was between FSR3 and DLSS3.

Why does this matter? Well, I can literally run DLSS4 on my RTX 4070 Ti Super, and get hugely better visual fidelity as a result. I can also turn on RT... I alternatively can use a more performant DLSS4 setting and get roughly the same visual fidelity as FSR4 using higher quality settings.

I'm seeing a 3.5% representation between the RTX 4070 Ti/Super and the RTX 4080/Super on Steam. I'm probably going to sell my RTX 4070 Ti Super for less than a RX 9070 costs....

It's super easy; barely an inconvenience, to get DLSS4 into a game as a gamer, not so much for FSR4, sadly. RT doesn't make a difference in every game, but the games it does are like WOW!

Seeing the difference between the upscalers gives me pause. Can an RTX 5070 deliver the same visual fidelity at balanced as an RTX 9070/XT can with FSR4 can at quality? What is the performance difference then? What about RT?

The RTX 5070 is in a weird place, but so is AMD. AMD needs to deliver significantly better value to gain market share, not simply match it. I still wouldn't be shocked to see the 9000 series only hit 1% combined on Steam....

text:
I mean I don't think that's true at all. For one it really can make a huge visual impact and in my opinion, when done well it's amazing. What is a fact though is that it can vastly simplify the lighting work that environment artists need to do. Obviously until RT becomes standard, they still have to do traditional lighting also so the workload isn't yet easier, but theoretically it will someday making lighting games much less complicated and tedious.

I will concede that the performance hit is rarely worth it, but I think that's for several reasons that will improve over time. One, some devs are amazing at fake lighting at this point, and two, the performance cost is so high that RT is often used very sparsely, and in many games is barely noticeable.

text: Please do not promote the cost per frame metric. As an indicator it holds absolutely no value. Allow me... 1) If MSRPs aren't yet a thing of the past, they are at the very least nearly impossible to come by. Not to mention a few months after a card gets released.  2) Other factors such as CPU, Memory speed, and even game settings, or the place in the game where testing was performed, will affect the game performance in ways that are non linear, making the CPR indicator only valid for the system it was tested and very hard to predict on a different setup. 3) The gaming consumer market does not value financially optimized decisions. We value performance more than we do money. CPR tries to make them both equal in importance, but a consumer will always try to buy the best card with the money they have in hand, and not the most cost effective card. We don't buy our cars based on cost per horse power, nor we buy vacuum cleaners based on cost per suction power or noise levels.

text: Do not purchase this graphics card. I'm not saying it's bad, but what pc gamers need to do is refuse doing business with companies who are 100% trying to take advantage of pc gamers by allowing price gouging. These companies are screwing pc gamers. The greed is on another level and it's disgusting. This might sound crazy, but I would not be surprised if the people you see on eBay scaling these new graphics cards are actually multiple people who are hired to sell these cards to make absurd profits. Think about it... Why is it that some people are able to sell dozens of these cards. Where did they get them? I do not believe it's bots buying up all these cards. Sure, there may be some able to get a few, but when you see an eBay seller with a significantly high level of repeated purchases, that is where things start to smell fishy to me. To be honest, it's the perfect plan. It's a genius way to screw their customers hiring people around the world selling these cards via bogus eBay accounts. Until these graphics card companies get their shit together, who actually has stock at launch on day 1 and being sold at MSRP, nobody should be doing business with these companies. I'm telling you guys, if pc gamers unite and say screw you Nvidia and AMD, we no longer are interested and are skipping this generation of graphics cards, I'd bet my life on it that the next generation of graphics cards will have so much stock on day 1 that it would blow peoples minds. The problem right now are the pc gamers who are caving into purchasing these cards for ridiculous prices, who know they are getting screwed, but they just have to have the latest and greatest cards. It's those people who are screwing up the market. These companies are targeting the pc gamers who are rich first, then once the rich pay those big bucks while sales start to settle down, only then will the average gamer finally be able to get their hands on these units. This price gouging money making scheme has got to stop. I know for a fact that there is something we don't know about. These cards should be on store shelves for launch, they are not on store shelves at launch, and that is all it really takes to come to the conclusion that these companies are doing something nefarious. This is just my 2 cents on the current matter. It really unfortunate for people to be getting screwed like this. These shortages should not be happening. Screw you AMD and Nvidia. I'll only do business with you when you finally start treating your customers better.

text: 9:34 I think i may know what's going on with the FFXIV data; DLSS and FSR are not made equal in this title. By default, not only does DLSS only kick in when below 60fps (with dynamic scaling, with no option to disable it unless always enabling DLSS), it uses DLSS3... While FSR uses FSR1, but it's set to 100% at default (with no dynamic scaling unless enabled), meaning it doesn't actually activate (same way that square implements their upscaling in their other titles, with janky "workarounds"). Could also be that the new cards arent really working correctly with it, i'm not sure... But that's my guess.

text:
So MSRP to MSRP $150 difference versus the TI, and yes I know actual pricing will be different, but that's likely on both sides. So they are still targeting that 20% mark as the incentive to Nvidia consumers. I dunno.. technically this should be their year to break out, unlikely to ever get a gift wrapped launch like this again, but I dunno. Traditionally the 20% hasn't been enough to move the needle with the system integrators, and that's who you really need to bag for market share. Typically SI's only go the AMD route when they can't find Nvidia stock. So maybe if Nvidia can't get cards to the SI... but aside from the death to Nvidia crowd I dunno if the traditional 20% is going to be enough. 

And that sucks, as much as I do prefer Nvidia's all around package (and typically just smoother running experience in my personal experience), I'd love to see them get some actual competition. Not really for pricing because I'm not naive enough to think AMD would be any better at pricing then they have in the past, and historically they've been just as bad even without any notable demand. Suddenly having demand wouldn't make them any better. More for the innovation it'd force. Like to see Nvidia push itself against more than just itself.

I dunno, I don't think 20% is enough to get them over the hump with the masses (or even the SIs) but maybe maybe with the supply issues if they can actually avoid the same mess? Maybe...

text:
@kerkertrandov459  FSR 4 is right behind DLSS 4 transformer, which is insanely good for their first hardware attempt, completely demolishing DLSS 3 or 4 without transformer.

DLAA, reflex, make Nvidia cards run worse than using standard DLSS or no reflex. Frame gen looks awful and is completely fake framerate - it's simulating a higher framerate, but the frames you're seeing are mostly not even real, and are interpolated creating after images and artifacts and frame time/input lag problems. Ray reconstruction, cuda, and anything else you talked about has basically nothing to do with benchmarks nor would change benchmarks for gaming. 

Also FSR 4 vs. DLSS 4 transformer have very similar performance losses compared to older upscaling models. 12 gb VRAM is a huge fucking problem in todays gaming. Good luck running anything at 4K with that without using upscaling or frame gen crutches or lowering settings. 

The main thing you brought up that even matters, as someone who currently uses Nvidia, is transformer, and it's not far off that it matters imo. 

Also something that you don't consider is that AMD is superior across the board on Linux compared to Nvidia, so take all these benchmarks and remove 10-20% performance from the Nvidia card and that's what it would be on Linux. AMD is open source so they actually get a 10-20% buff on Linux compared to Windows.

NVIDIA is reinventing the lighting wheel (RT) to sell you its proprietary solution (DLSS). It might be better in the future but it's still poorly optimized, way too demanding for no true benefits to actual users. It only serves to enable lazy devs at the moment.

author: @s3rit661

text:
@s3rit661  Except it is, bc it functions the same on both cards? Fsr is an amd technology, but it isn't like Intel's xess where it works differently on intel and non Intel cards, it always works the same. Fsr 4 will change that, but these results don't use fsr 4 as it is not released yet. 

As for not using fsr at all, that might not be an option, as some games force fsr/dlss on to serve as a temporal AA pass in order to reduce the noisy artifacts that rt can produce.
author: @idrinkbbq5927

text: @idrinkbbq5927  It does not "function" the same on both cards, if by "function" you mean use the hardware in the same way, FSR works "better" on AMD hardware or viceversa sometimes (and i'm not talking about FSR 4), if you take 2 benchmarks one with rast and one with FSR, of both a nvidia and AMD gpu, you'll see different gains in %. It make sense anyway to isolate the RT performances to have a clear view on who's higher on RT perfomances (and that's Nvidia). In the case where you cannot isolate, then you can simply show DLSS and FSR for nvidia (without FG or MFG) and FSR for AMD "RT performances"
author: @s3rit661

text: @s3rit661  that argument falls apart as soon as you bring other cards from either side into the mix. A 5070 and a 9070 xt will have different amounts of performance gained from fsr, sure. But so will a 5080, or a 7900 xtx. They all behave slightly differently with upscaling tech, which is unfortunate, but the result is consistent. As this is a benchmark, consistency and repeatability are both incredibly important. Is it perfectly representative of how an end user would use their 5070 ti, to run cp2077 with high ass rt settings but use fsr? No, they would likely use dlss, and I'm totally agreeing with you there. But for a benchmark, it is better to have the consistency of settings used, as it is a more level field for x card vs y card, rather than introducing more variables into the results that make them incomparable to each other directly.
